title: The Brocklesby mid-air collision, 1940 — two Ansons locked together land as one
sources: Wikipedia: 1940 Brocklesby mid-air collision — 29 September 1940; two RAAF Avro Ansons of No. 2 Service Flying Training School, cross-country training exercise over southern New South Wales; 300 m (1,000 ft) over Brocklesby, banking turn; Fuller (22, upper Anson N4876) lost sight of Hewson's aircraft beneath him; collided and remained jammed together; upper aircraft's engines knocked out, lower one's at full power; both navigators and the lower pilot Hewson bailed out; Fuller controlled the pair with ailerons and flaps; emergency belly landing in a paddock south-west of Brocklesby; all four crewmen survived; Fuller promoted to sergeant but confined to barracks for fourteen days and docked seven days' pay for speaking to newspapers without authorisation
Wikipedia: Avro Anson — Ansons L9162 and N4876 of No. 2 SFTS RAAF collided and became locked together in flight; emergency landing at Brocklesby, New South Wales

post.facebook:
On this day in 1940, two planes collided in mid-air — and landed as one.

Two Avro Ansons of an Australian flying school were on a cross-country training exercise over New South Wales. Over the town of Brocklesby they made a banking turn, and the upper pilot, 22-year-old Leonard Fuller, lost sight of the plane beneath him.

They collided and jammed together. The top plane's engines were knocked out; the bottom plane's kept running at full power. Both navigators and the lower pilot bailed out.

Fuller stayed. He found he could still control the pair with his ailerons and flaps, picked a paddock, and made a belly landing. All four men survived, and both aircraft were repaired.

Fuller was promoted to sergeant — and confined to barracks for fourteen days for speaking to the newspapers without permission.
